newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British service sector shows strong growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British service sector shows strong growth.

text.p: Business conditions in the British services sector showed a significant improvement in May, providing further evidence that interest rates may need to rise, according to a leading business survey published on Wednesday.
The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said its business activity index rose to a new seasonally adjusted high of 64.8 from 61.2 in April, the 11th consecutive monthly increase.
"The rise in activity reflected an increase in the number of firms found to have been boosting capacity to meet strengthening demand for their services," the CIPS said.
"The rate of growth of incoming new business has picked up significantly over the past seven months and accelerated again in May to record the largest monthly rise reported to date."
The survey, sponsored by Reuters, is based on information from 500 executives in private sector service industries, excluding retail and wholesale.

Economists said the survey showed the service sector, which account for around two-thirds of gross domestic product (GDP), was booming, in contrast to manufacturers, who are struggling to export because of the strength of the pound.

It was likely to provide further encouragement to the Bank of England's monetary policy committee, newly empowered to set interest rates, to raise the cost of borrowing when it meets on Thursday and Friday.

"Since services is a much more important sector of the economy than manufacturing, this report should be seen as a better guide to overall economic performance," said Jeremy Hawkins, an economist at Bank of America.

"The survey is unambiguously strong and must be seen as increasing the risk of a Bank of England tightening at the end of the week. All of the components showed solid gains and both of the key price elements were too high for comfort."
Official interest rates are raised to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent last month. The central bank has subsequently warned that they are likely to have to rise further to keep inflation down.
The services survey showed average input prices at the highest level so far.

"Rising wages and salaries were the principal cause of higher costs in May, with a shortage of suitably qualified staff again driving wages higher in many sectors, especially computing," the CIPS said.
Employment rose strongly for the 11th month in a row, reflecting companies' need to expand capacity to meet current and anticipated future growth in demand for services.
Respondents generally expected business conditions to improve over the next year, driven largely by continued growth in the economy and especially by greater consumer spending on services.
Increasing numbers of service companies were reported to have raised their charges to maintain profit margins.
"On the whole, prices charged rose for the seventh consecutive month, with a modest acceleration in the rate of increase," the CIPS said.
However, strong competition continued to limit firms' ability to raise prices.
"Although a fifth of all companies reported a rise in costs, only 12 percent of companies were able to raise their charges."
